blocks.text: A mission states the business’s purpose and the value it seeks to provide. Objectives translate direction into outcomes that can guide action and evaluation. Useful objectives are clear, measurable, realistic and time-bound while remaining relevant to the strategy.

Illustrative objective: achieve 500 repeat overseas customers within 12 months while maintaining a defined service standard and contribution margin. This is more useful than “be successful globally” because management can assess progress and trade-offs.

Environmental scanning gathers and interprets information about factors affecting the business. PEST examines political and legal, economic, socio-cultural and technological conditions. Focus on relevant changes and explain their business consequences.

For an exporter, a currency movement may affect margins, a new labelling rule may delay entry and a shift in purchasing preferences may alter demand. A list of factors without analysis does not establish which strategy the business should adopt.

Porter’s Five Forces analyses industry competition: rivalry among existing competitors, threat of new entrants, threat of substitute products or services, bargaining power of buyers and bargaining power of suppliers. Together they help assess pressure on profitability.

A substitute meets a similar need in a different way; it is not simply another brand of the same product. Entry barriers, switching costs, differentiation and concentration can affect the strength of the forces. Apply the model to a defined industry and market.

rows: Number of rivals, growth and differentiation
Capital, scale, regulation and brand barriers

blocks.text: The model identifies competitive pressures rather than predicting a precise profit. Consider how the business can respond and whether the opportunity fits its capabilities.

SWOT distinguishes internal strengths and weaknesses from external opportunities and threats. Evidence should be specific to the business and its objective. A strength is useful when it helps the firm respond to the relevant environment.

Move from lists to strategies: use a strength to exploit an opportunity, address a weakness preventing entry, use a strength to reduce a threat, or reduce exposure where weaknesses and threats combine. For example, strong design capability may support differentiation, while a weak distribution network may require a partner.

Formulation develops and compares courses of action that could achieve the objectives. Evaluate fit with the environment, capabilities, costs, risks and stakeholder effects. Choose a clear direction rather than a collection of unrelated activities.

A business might compare direct exporting, a distributor and a joint venture. Explain why the selected approach offers the strongest fit and what must be true for it to work. Document assumptions and contingency options.

Implementation puts the strategy into action through responsibilities, budgets, schedules, systems and people. Translate broad choices into coordinated departmental plans and measurable milestones. Communication and change support help employees understand their role.

For a new distribution partnership, implementation includes contracts, inventory arrangements, training, product information and escalation procedures. A plan that omits ownership of tasks can fail even when the underlying strategy is sound.

Evaluation compares actual performance with objectives and investigates differences. Control involves corrective action where needed. Use financial and non-financial indicators, reliable data and an appropriate review schedule.

Lower costs may appear favourable while complaints and late deliveries rise. Interpret the measures together and investigate causes. Management may change execution, allocate resources differently or revise the strategy when evidence challenges its assumptions.

Financial ratios relate figures from financial statements to help assess liquidity, profitability and stability. Owners, lenders, suppliers and managers use them to support decisions. A ratio summarises part of performance; it does not explain every cause or predict success.

Compare relevant periods and suitable industry benchmarks using consistent definitions. Accounting policies, estimates, seasonality and unusual transactions can affect comparisons. Combine financial analysis with cash-flow information and non-financial evidence.

Assets are resources controlled by the business; liabilities are obligations; equity is the residual interest after liabilities. The accounting equation is assets = liabilities + equity. Current and non-current classifications help distinguish the timing and nature of resources and obligations.

A balance sheet reports financial position at a date. An income statement reports income and expenses over a period. A cash-flow statement reports cash movements. Profit is not the same as cash, and retained earnings are not necessarily available cash.

rows: Total assets / total liabilities / equity at end

blocks.text: This simplified teaching example assumes no additional income, interest or tax adjustments. Gross profit is net sales less cost of goods sold; profit is gross profit less the stated operating expenses. Total assets equal liabilities plus equity.

Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities. In the example, $60,000 ÷ $30,000 = 2:1. There are $2 of current assets for each $1 of current liabilities at the reporting date. This provides an indication of short-term financial coverage.

A commonly taught 2:1 guide is not a universal ideal. Inventory may be slow to sell and receivables may be overdue. A high ratio can also suggest underused resources. Assess asset quality, the timing of payments and industry conditions.

Gross profit ratio = gross profit ÷ net sales × 100 when expressed as a percentage. Here, $80,000 ÷ $200,000 × 100 = 40%. For each dollar of net sales, 40 cents remain after cost of goods sold, before the other expenses in this example.

A falling ratio may reflect higher input costs, lower selling prices, discounting or a changed sales mix. Investigate the cause before recommending a response. Supplier negotiations or pricing changes can affect quality and demand as well as margin.

Profit ratio = profit ÷ net sales × 100. Here, $30,000 ÷ $200,000 × 100 = 15%. In this example, 15 cents of each dollar of net sales become profit after the stated costs. Use the profit definition and reporting period given in the question.

A low ratio may reflect weak gross margin, high operating expenses or unusual costs. Increasing sales does not automatically increase the ratio. Compare performance with prior periods and a relevant benchmark, then explain the likely business consequences.

Expense ratio = operating expenses ÷ net sales × 100. Here, $50,000 ÷ $200,000 × 100 = 25%. Operating expenses absorb 25 cents of each dollar of net sales. Do not add cost of goods sold again when it is separate from the specified operating expenses.

A rising ratio can result from higher expenses or weaker sales. Lower is not always better: cutting essential training or maintenance may damage later performance. In this simplified dataset, gross profit ratio minus expense ratio equals profit ratio: 40% − 25% = 15%.

For this syllabus, return on equity ratio = profit ÷ equity at end × 100. Here, $30,000 ÷ $120,000 × 100 = 25%. It relates the period’s profit to closing equity. Some other contexts use average equity, so follow the prescribed definition.

A change can result from profit or equity movements. Greater borrowing can raise the apparent return on equity while increasing risk. The ratio is not a guaranteed dividend or the same as a shareholder’s total market investment return. A zero or negative denominator requires special care.

Debt to equity ratio = total liabilities ÷ total equity. Here, $80,000 ÷ $120,000 = 0.67:1, approximately, or 66.67% if expressed as a percentage. Liabilities are about 67 cents for each dollar of equity. Use the total-liabilities definition prescribed for this course.

A higher ratio generally indicates greater reliance on liabilities relative to equity and can increase financial risk. It does not by itself prove insolvency. Assess repayment timing, cash flows, asset quality and industry conditions. Borrowing can support productive investment, but returns are uncertain.

rows: Will assets become cash before debts fall due?
Are input costs and pricing sustainable?
Which costs explain the final margin?
How do profit and financing affect the result?
Can cash flow support the obligations?

blocks.text: Use the figures to support a judgement, not as a substitute for one. A business can report profit and still face a cash shortage.

State the formula, substitute the correct figures, show the result with an appropriate unit and explain what it means for the case. When comparing percentages, distinguish percentage points from relative percentage change.

Illustrative example: profit ratio falls from 18% to 15%, a fall of 3 percentage points. Investigate cost and sales changes before recommending a response. An unsupported claim that every margin below a fixed percentage is poor ignores industry and business context.

Production management systems coordinate the transformation of inputs into goods or services. They help plan resources, schedule activities, monitor progress and control cost, quality and delivery. Inputs can include people, materials, equipment, information and finance.

A service business also manages production: a repair firm schedules technicians, parts and customer appointments. The system should support the business’s competitive priorities rather than maximise output regardless of customer need.

Forecast demand, determine capacity and arrange the resources needed to meet expected orders. Scheduling sets the sequence and timing of work. Capacity planning considers bottlenecks, equipment, skills and available time.

Too little capacity can cause delays and lost sales; excess capacity creates cost without matching revenue. Forecasts are uncertain, so consider flexibility and contingency arrangements. A single bottleneck can limit the output of an entire process.

Track output, defects, lead times, resource use and delivery performance. Compare results with plans and investigate variation. Accurate information allows managers to adjust schedules, suppliers or processes before a small problem becomes widespread.

Higher utilisation can reduce spare capacity available for urgent orders or maintenance. Balance efficiency with resilience, quality and safety. A system that produces quickly but creates excessive rework may increase total cost.

International operations add transport lead times, time zones, supplier dependencies and differing standards. Coordinate specifications, information and quality expectations across locations. Consider the full cost rather than labour cost alone.

Illustrative case: offshore assembly lowers unit labour cost but increases freight, lead time and inventory. Evaluate landed cost, defect risk and responsiveness before choosing the location. Use performance data to review whether expected savings occur.

bme-y12-u4-product-development.title: From customer need to a viable offer

blocks.text: Product development turns an opportunity into a product or service that can be produced, delivered and supported. It may involve a new offer or an improvement to an existing one. Customer value, technical feasibility and commercial viability need to fit together.
A feature is useful when it addresses a relevant need. More features can add complexity and cost without improving value. Begin with evidence about customers and the problem to be solved.

Generate ideas from research, employees, customers, suppliers and technology. Screen them against objectives, capability, costs and market potential. Develop a concept and assess demand, competitors, risks and expected financial outcomes.

An idea can be attractive but unsuitable for the business’s resources. Document assumptions and test the most uncertain ones before committing large amounts. Global feasibility also includes cultural fit, local standards and distribution.

Develop prototypes or service trials, test performance and gather feedback from relevant users. Refine design, materials, usability and production methods. Plan quality checks, supplier readiness, staff training, pricing and communication before launch.

A limited launch can expose practical problems while reducing the scale of failure. Testing should be representative and should not rely only on enthusiastic early users. Include support and returns arrangements in the design.

After launch, assess adoption, repeat purchase, returns, defects and contribution. Compare actual results with assumptions and identify whether problems arise from design, positioning, price or delivery.

Illustrative example: customers like a reusable container but find its seal difficult to clean. Redesign and retesting may improve satisfaction more than additional advertising. Feed evidence back into development instead of treating launch as the final stage.

Quality concerns how well a product, service or process meets defined requirements and customer expectations. It includes reliable performance and consistency, rather than simply a premium appearance. Clear specifications make it possible to evaluate results.

Poor quality creates rework, returns, complaints and reputational damage. Prevention and improvement can have costs but reduce wider failure costs. Consider customer needs, safety and the business’s value proposition.

Quality control checks outputs or stages of production against standards to identify defects. Inspection, testing and sampling can detect problems before products reach customers. A service business might review completed work or sample recorded interactions.
Detection does not necessarily prevent recurrence. Sampling can miss defects, while checking every output can be costly. Define what happens to failed outputs and investigate the underlying process.

Quality assurance establishes planned processes intended to give confidence that requirements will be met consistently. It emphasises prevention through documented procedures, training, supplier standards and appropriate checks.

A food producer may use controlled handling procedures, calibrated equipment and staff training. Documentation alone is insufficient if practice differs. Audit and feedback help verify whether the system is followed and effective.

Quality improvement uses evidence to make products and processes better over time. Identify a problem, investigate causes, test a change, review results and standardise a successful improvement. Employee and customer feedback can reveal issues that output inspection misses.

Illustrative example: recurring packaging leaks lead the team to identify inconsistent sealing temperature. A controlled adjustment and monitoring reduce defects. Improvement addresses the cause rather than repeatedly discarding failed products.

rows: Train staff and maintain calibrated equipment
Analyse leaks and refine the sealing method

blocks.text: These approaches complement one another. Evaluate defect rates, rework, complaints and total quality costs, while checking that changes preserve safety and customer value.
